a: until you are just like them
p: One codex repeats 'be afraid' instead of the doubled 'become like'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete, with Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD)
readings.en: having become like the foreigners, you become like (them)
readings.plain: until you are just like them

readings.w: Codex Marchalianus (Q, 500s AD), in Swete's notes
readings.en: having become like the foreigners, you be afraid

why: Vaticanus and Alexandrinus agree, and the doubled verb is the harder reading; Q's 'be afraid' looks like a copyist's anticipation of the fear in the next clause.

a: Say instead, in your own mind, "You are the one we must worship, Master."
t: The prayer missing in one codex
p: Codex Alexandrinus leaves out the captives' silent prayer.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete, with Codex Marchalianus (Q); the Vulgate and the KJV
readings.orig: εἴπατε δὲ τῇ διανοίᾳ Σοὶ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν, Δέσποτα.
readings.en: but say in the mind: To you it is necessary to bow down, Master.
readings.plain: Say instead, in your own mind, "You are the one we must worship, Master."

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD), in Swete's notes

why: Every other witness has the prayer, and 6:6 ('For my angel is with you') follows from it. The gap in Alexandrinus is most likely an accidental skip.

a: he himself is looking after your lives
p: Swete notes no Greek variant here. The Latin, and the KJV after it, make God say 'I myself'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete (Swete notes no other reading here)
readings.orig: αὐτός τε ἐκζητῶν τὰς ψυχὰς ὑμῶν
readings.en: and he himself seeking out your souls
readings.plain: he himself is looking after your lives

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (ipse autem exquiram animas vestras), with the Douay-Rheims ('I myself will demand an account of your souls') and the KJV ('I myself caring for your souls')
readings.en: and I myself will seek out your souls
readings.plain: I myself will look after your lives

why: Swete notes no other Greek reading: this is a difference between the Greek and the Latin, not between Greek manuscripts. The Plain follows the Greek, where the participle is third person and goes with the angel.
b: The verb ekzēteō can mean to seek out with care, or to call to account, as God will "demand a reckoning" for a person's life (Genesis 9:5, where the Greek has the same verb); the Douay-Rheims takes the second sense. Both senses are open. The Plain takes the caring sense, since the verse follows the promise of the angel's company; that is a choice from the context, not from the word.

p: Swete's text has a present verb here; three other codices have the aorist used in the other refrains.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete
readings.en: so do not fear them (present tense)

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Marchalianus (Q) and the codex Swete marks Γ, in Swete's notes
readings.orig: ηφοβηθητε (Swete's note, exactly as printed: φοβεισθε] ηφοβηθητε AQΓ)
readings.en: do not fear (aorist, the form of the other refrains), if the first letter is a slip (see below)
readings.plain: So have no fear of them.

why: The Plain follows its base text, Vaticanus. The other reading matches the aorist phobēthēte that Swete's text has in the refrains at 6:14, 6:28, 6:64 and 6:68.
b: The reading is given here exactly as the digital text of Swete's notes prints it, ηφοβηθητε. The first η is probably a stray character in that text: the same η stands before the word φερονται in his note on 6:25, where it cannot belong to the word. Read without it, the reading is the aorist φοβηθητε. At 6:68 Swete's note reports that the first hand of Q wrote ςφοβητε there, corrected to φοβηθητε (Qa).

a: so what future do the things they made have?
p: Codex Alexandrinus adds 'be gods', and the KJV follows that sense.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: πῶς τε δὴ μέλλει τὰ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν κατασκευασθέντα;
readings.en: and how indeed are the things made by them going to (be)?
readings.plain: so what future do the things they made have?

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (adds εἶναι θεοί), in Swete's notes; the Vulgate; the KJV ('how should then the things that are made of them be gods?')
readings.orig: πῶς οὖν μέλλει τὰ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν κατασκευασθέντα εἶναι θεοί;
readings.en: how then are the things made by them going to be gods?
readings.plain: so how could the things they made be gods?

why: The short reading is harder, since the verb has no infinitive, and Alexandrinus looks like a copyist filling the gap with the letter's theme. The sense of Vaticanus fits 6:46: the makers do not last long, so their work has no future either.

a: Who is there, then, who still has to learn that they are not gods?
t: Who needs to learn, or who cannot know?
p: Two codices add 'not', which gives the KJV's 'Who then may not know that they are no gods?'

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Τίνι οὖν γνωστέον ἐστὶν ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί;
readings.en: To whom, then, is it (still) to be made known that they are not gods?
readings.plain: Who is there, then, who still has to learn that they are not gods?

readings.w: Codex Marchalianus (Q, οὐ γνωστέον) and Codex Alexandrinus (γνωστὸν ... οὐκ ἔσται), in Swete's notes; the KJV
readings.orig: Τίνι οὖν οὐ γνωστέον ἐστὶν ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί;
readings.en: To whom, then, is it not to be known that they are not gods?
readings.plain: Who, then, can fail to know that they are not gods?

why: Both readings make the same rhetorical point. The Plain keeps its base text; the added 'not' in two codices smooths the question.

p: Vaticanus has a verb that does not fit. Alexandrinus and Marchalianus say 'be saved'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete (his note gives other readings only for A and Q)
readings.en: they will never 'set' or 'arrange' (from diatithēmi; the verb makes little sense here)

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (διασώσουσιν) and Codex Marchalianus (Q, first hand, διασωθῶσιν), in Swete's notes; the Vulgate (se liberabunt) and the KJV ('able to escape')
readings.en: they will never bring (themselves) safely through / be brought safely through

why: The Plain departs from its base text here. Vaticanus' διαθῶσιν does not give good sense and is probably a slip for a form of διασῴζω, 'bring safely through', which the other codices have and which the letter uses at 6:11, 6:54 and 6:58.

p: Swete prints the word as Marchalianus spells it, since Vaticanus misspells it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (συκηράτῳ) and Codex Alexandrinus (συκηεράτῳ), in Swete's notes

why: Sikyēraton, from sikys 'cucumber', is the word the Greek of Isaiah 1:8 uses for the cucumber field. Vaticanus and Alexandrinus spell it with sy-, a copying slip, and Swete corrects his base text here from Q. The meaning does not change.

p: Every Greek copy in Swete's notes says 'marble', which does not rot. The Vulgate has purple and murex, eaten by moths.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, as printed by Swete, with Alexandrinus and Marchalianus (Swete notes no other reading for this word)
Latin Vulgate (a purpura quoque et murice, quae supra illos tineant, 'the purple and murex, which are moth-eaten upon them'); the Douay-Rheims 'scarlet'

why: The Plain follows the Greek, its base text, even though marble does not rot. The Latin differs: it has purple and murex, the shellfish that gives purple dye, and says they are moth-eaten.
b: Carey Moore explained the oddity by a Hebrew original: the Hebrew word for 'alabaster' or 'marble', shesh, has a homograph that means 'fine linen', and a translator who chose the wrong one would give 'marble' where the writer meant linen, which does rot. Benjamin Wright, introducing the NETS translation, reports this argument; NETS still translates 'marble', because it renders the Greek as it stands. It is a theory about a lost Hebrew text, not a reading found in any copy.
